The district court also relied on a four-page declaration by Kenneth 
Pahnkas, President of the National Citizenship and Immigration Services 
Council (the union representing USCIS employees processing DACA 
apphcations), for the proposition that “DACA applications are simply 
rubberstamped if the appEcants meet the necessary criteria.” Yet lay 
witness conclusions are only competent evidence if rationally drawn from 
facts personally observed. See Fed.R.Evid. 701. Here, Palinkas’s conclusion 
was supported only by the fact that DACA applications are routed to 
“service centers instead of field offices,” and that ‘TJSCIS officers in service 
centers ... do not interview applicants”—a weak basis on which to conclude 
that DHS’s representations (both to the public and to the courts) are 
“merely pretext.” Indeed, Pahnkas’s assertions are rebutted—and the step- 
by-step process for reviewing DACA applications is explained—^in the 
detailed affidavit filed by Donald Neufeld, the head of those very USCIS 
service centers. Neufeld declares that the service centers “are designed to 
adjudicate apphcations, petitions and requests” for various programs “that 
have higher-volume caseloads.” Neufeld goes on to describe the “multi-step, 
case-specific process” for reviewing DACA apphcations: “Once a case 
arrives at a Service Center, a specially trained USCIS adjudicator is 
assigned to determine whether the requestor satisfies the DACA guidelines 
J
and ultimately determine whether a request should be approved or 
denied.” Adjudicators “evaluate the evidence each requestor submits in 
conjunction with the relevant DACA guidehnes” and “assess the 
appropriate weight to accord such evidence.” Citing various examples, 
Neufeld explains that “[e]ven if it is determined that a requestor has 
satisfied the threshold DACA guidehnes, USCIS may exercise discretion to 
deny a request where other factors make the grant of deferred action 
inappropriate.” As a part of their review, adjudicators can investigate the 
facts and evidence supporting the application ‘"by contacting educational 
institutions, other government agencies, employers, or other entities.” 
Moreover, although the Pahnkas Declaration accurately states that 
adjudicators at USCIS service centers do not have the capabihty to 
interview apphcants, the Neufeld Declaration clarifies that service center 
adjudicators “may refer a case for interview at a Field Office”—^for example, 
“when the adjudicator determines, after careful review of the request and 
supporting documents, that a request is deniable, but potentially curable, 
with information that can best be received through an interview.” 
Adjudicators may also request that apphcants submit additional evidence 
in support of their apphcations for deferred action; this was no rare 
occurrence, as nearly 200,000 such requests for additional evidence were 
issued by adjudicators. * * *
* * * At a minimum * * *, the Neufeld Declaration created a factual 
dispute warranting an evidentiary hearing. The district court’s failure to 
hold an evidentiary hearing further undermines faith in its factual 
conclusions.
